items.text: In  today's  digital  age,  convenience  often  comes  at  the  cost of privacy.  Every  time  a  user  browses  a  website,  clicks  a  link,  or uses  an  app,  their  data  is  collected  -sometimes  without their knowledge. Companies  use  this  information  to  target  ads, predict behavior, or even sell insights to third parties. While this can lead to better services, it also raises ethical concerns. Who controls this data? How is it stored, and can users truly opt out? Many people accept terms and conditions without reading them, unknowingly giving permission for data tracking. Some countries have passed laws to protect user data, but implementation remains weak. As surveillance tools grow smarter,  the  line  between  public  and  private  becomes  blurred. Individuals must now learn to balance the benefits of technology with the right to privacy-a task  that  requires  awareness, regulation, and responsible digital behavior.

items.text:
Artificial  Intelligence  (AI)  is  gradually  transforming  the  way students  learn.  From  virtual  tutors  to  personalized  learning paths, AI helps identify each learner's strengths and weaknesses.  With  the  help  of  data,  AI  systems  can  suggest specific  topics  where  students need improvement. Schools are also  using  AI  chatbots  to  answer  basic  queries,  reducing  the pressure on teachers. However, experts warn that over-dependence on AI may limit critical thinking. If students rely too much on machines for answers, they may lose problem-solving  skills.  There  are  also  concerns  about  data privacy,  especially  when  student  performance  data  is  stored online. Despite these issues, many educators believe AI can be a useful tool when used wisely. Like any technology, the key lies in balancing human guidance with machine efficiency.
